title: Patricia Neal
wiki_lead: Patricia Neal (born Patsy Louise Neal; January 20, 1926 – August 8, 2010) was an American actress of stage and screen. She is well known for, among other roles, playing World War II widow Helen Benson in The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951), radio journalist Marcia Jeffries in A Face in the Crowd (1957), wealthy matron Emily Eustace Failenson in Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961), and the worn-out housekeeper Alma Brown in Hud (1963) (for which she won the Academy Award for Best Actress). She also featured as the matriarch in the television film The Homecoming: A Christmas Story (1971); her role as Olivia Walton was re-cast for the series it inspired, The Waltons. A major star of the 1950s and 1960s, she was the recipient of an Academy Award, a Golden Globe Award, a Tony Award, and two British Academy Film Awards, and was nominated for three Primetime Emmy Awards.
wiki_excerpt:
Patricia Neal (born Patsy Louise Neal; January 20, 1926 – August 8, 2010) was an American actress of stage and screen. She is well known for, among other roles, playing World War II widow Helen Benson in The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951), radio journalist Marcia Jeffries in A Face in the Crowd (1957), wealthy matron Emily Eustace Failenson in Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961), and the worn-out housekeeper Alma Brown in Hud (1963) (for which she won the Academy Award for Best Actress). She also featured as the matriarch in the television film The Homecoming: A Christmas Story (1971); her role as Olivia Walton was re-cast for the series it inspired, The Waltons. A major star of the 1950s and 1960s, she was the recipient of an Academy Award, a Golden Globe Award, a Tony Award, and two British Academy Film Awards, and was nominated for three Primetime Emmy Awards.


Early life and education
Neal was born in Packard, Whitley County, Kentucky, to William Burdette Neal and Eura Mildred (née Petrey) Neal. She had two siblings.
Neal grew up in Knoxville, Tennessee, where she attended Knoxville High School, and studied drama at Northwestern, where she was a member of Pi Beta Phi sorority. At Northwestern, she was crowned Syllabus Queen in a campus-wide beauty pageant. She left Northwestern after talent scouts convinced her to leave for New York.


Career
Neal gained her first job in New York as an understudy in the Broadway production of the John Van Druten play The Voice of the Turtle. Next, she appeared in Lillian Hellman's Another Part of the Forest (1946), winning the 1947 Tony Award for Best Featured Actress in a Play, in the first presentation of the Tony awards.
Neal made her film debut with Ronald Reagan in John Loves Mary in 1949, followed by another role with Reagan in The Hasty Heart the same year. Her work in The Fountainhead, which was released in 1949, coincided with her affair with married co-star Gary Cooper; she worked with him again in Bright Leaf (1950).

Neal starred with John Garfield in The Breaking Point (1950), in The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951) with Michael Rennie, and in Operation Pacific (also 1951) starring John Wayne. She suffered a nervous breakdown around this time, following the end of her relationship with Gary Cooper, and departed Hollywood for New York, returning to Broadway in 1952 for a revival of The Children's Hour. In 1955, she starred in Edith Sommer's A Roomful of Roses, staged by Guthrie McClintic.

While in New York, Neal became a member of the Actors Studio. Based on connections with other members, she subsequently co-starred in the film A Face in the Crowd (1957, directed by Elia Kazan), the play The Miracle Worker (1959, directed by Arthur Penn), the film Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961), and the film Hud (1963), directed by Martin Ritt and starring Paul Newman. grok_lead: Patricia Neal (January 20, 1926 â August 8, 2010) was an acclaimed American actress whose career spanned stage, film, and television, marked by an Academy Award for Best Actress for her role in Hud (1963) and a Tony Award for her Broadway debut in Another Part of the Forest (1946), while enduring profound personal tragedies including the deaths of a daughter and severe strokes that tested her resilience. Born Patsy Lou Neal in Packard, Kentucky, she was the daughter of a coal company manager and relocated with her family to Knoxville, Tennessee, at a young age, where she developed an early passion for theater. After graduating from Knoxville High School in 1943, Neal briefly attended Northwestern University's School of Speech for two years, studying under acting instructor Alvina Krause, before leaving to pursue professional opportunities in New York City. Neal's stage career launched dramatically in 1946 when, at age 20, she understudied in The Voice of the Turtle and soon starred in Lillian Hellman's Another Part of the Forest, earning a Tony Award for Best Featured Actress in a Playâthe inaugural year of the awardsâand the Drama Critics' Circle Award. She transitioned to film in 1949 with her debut in The Fountainhead opposite Gary Cooper, followed by notable roles in The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951) as the love interest to an alien visitor, A Face in the Crowd (1957) directed by Elia Kazan, and a supporting part as 2E Failenson in Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961). Her portrayal of the strong-willed housekeeper Alma Brown in Hud brought her widespread acclaim and the Oscar, solidifying her status as a leading actress of the era, though she later reflected on the role's moral ambiguity as a departure from her typical characters. In her personal life, Neal married British author Roald Dahl on July 2, 1953, after meeting him in 1949; the couple had five childrenâOlivia Twenty, Theo Matthew, Tessa, Ophelia, and Lucy âbut faced devastating losses, including Theo's severe brain injury from a 1960 New York taxi accident that caused hydrocephalus, and Olivia's death at age seven in 1962 from measles encephalitis. In 1965, while pregnant with Lucy, Neal suffered three massive strokes that left her in a three-week coma, partially paralyzed on her right side, and with slurred speech; under Dahl's rigorous rehabilitation regimen, she relearned to walk and talk within months, though recovery took years. She returned to acting in 1968, earning an Oscar nomination for The Subject Was Roses and continuing with stage productions like The Miracle Worker (1959) and films such as Cookie's Fortune (1999), while also appearing on television, including an Emmy-nominated role in The Homecoming: A Christmas Story (1971). Neal and Dahl divorced in 1983 after 30 years, amid reported strains from her health struggles and his affair, but she remained close to their family, including granddaughter Sophie Dahl, a model and author. A dedicated advocate for stroke and paralysis recovery, she established the Patricia Neal Rehabilitation Center in Knoxville in 1978, which became a leading facility for neurological rehabilitation, and authored the autobiography As I Am (1988) detailing her ordeals. Neal received further honors, including a Golden Globe for The Homecoming, BAFTA Awards for Hud, and recognition as one of America's ten most admired women in 1970; her final film role was in Flying By (2009). She died of lung cancer on August 8, 2010, at her home in Edgartown, Massachusetts, at age 84, leaving a legacy of artistic achievement and inspirational fortitude.
